articles.title: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Changes the Film’s Ending — The Russo Brothers Explain Why They Went Back
articles.summary: "The idea of just going one moment past that perfect ending, and thinking about how radically that moment can change," Anthony Russo explains
articles.body:
The following story contains spoilers for "Avengers: Endgame Encore."

With "Avengers: Endgame Encore," Marvel primed fans for the story of "Avengers: Doomsday."

Directors Joe and Anthony Russo included four new scenes in the theatrical re-release, warming up viewers for Robert Downey Jr.'s villainous turn in "Doomsday." One moment in particular that the Russo brothers intentionally changed in "Endgame" was the "perfect ending" for Steve Rogers.

Anthony Russo said that he and his brother gave themselves the creative limitation that "Endgame" truly was the ending for the character when making the film in the 2010s. But the pair decided to alter that original conclusion with "Encore."

"It was many years later before the idea – this idea, that we actually committed to – came up, on how to move past that moment," Anthony Russo said in an interview with Empire . "A big motivation for releasing 'Avengers: Endgame Encore' is the idea that, now we're looking back at that movie thinking about going forward."

The directors shared that they used all of the same lighting, lenses and sets to make the new footage fit naturally within the "Endgame" scenes filmed years ago.

"The idea of just going one moment past that perfect ending, and thinking about how radically that moment can change by just taking one step past it," Anthony Russo said. "That was a big part of the delight in the new idea for what Doomsday is and where the story goes."

In "Encore," the new ending shows Loki (Tom Hiddleston) appearing to Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) and Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell). In the first official trailer for "Avengers: Doomsday," Loki can be seen giving somebody his card from the TVA, or Time Variance Authority (more on that later). It now seems likely that he gave that card to Steve

Before the events of "Endgame Encore," Loki sacrificed his life in his self-titled Disney+ show to become the God of Stories, protecting the multiverse at the end of time.

"The Marvel Universe is a giant experiment, and has been for years. I think part of the fun of coming back was, we thought, 'Could we reach back to pull the story forward?' And nobody's done that before," Joe Russo said on the new ending. "Nobody's ever had an opportunity to do it before."

As for Loki's appearance in the film, the creators did clarify that the new scenes were shot specifically to bridge the gap ahead of "Doomsday," and that Loki's presences is part of that.

"Look, the God of Mischief proves to be the God of Mischief," Anthony said. "Loki's one of the most fascinating characters, and he's had so many incarnations. One of the delights of 'Doomsday' is, you're going to get a new incarnation of that character."

"Avengers: Doomsday" will release in theaters nationwide on Dec. 18. The Russo brothers directed the film, starring Downey Jr. as Victor von Doom with Chris Evans, Chris Hemsworth and a bounty of other returning Marvel stars.

articles.summary: Seleção que oferece vagas remanescentes considera notas do Enem de 2016 a 2025 e tem inscrições gratuitas pela internet.
articles.body:
Praça do RU na UFMT, em Cuiabá — Foto: UFMT/Divulgação

A Universidade Federal de Mato Grosso (UFMT) está com inscrições abertas para o processo seletivo que oferece 967 vagas remanescentes em cursos de graduação presenciais nos câmpus de Cuiabá , Várzea Grande , Sinop e Araguaia até domingo (4). As vagas são destinadas ao segundo semestre letivo de 2026 .

Do total, 783 vagas são para ampla concorrência e 184 para estudantes que cursaram o ensino médio em escolas públicas. A seleção ocorre por meio das notas do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem).

Em Cuiabá, são 320 vagas, com 248 para ampla concorrência e 72 para escolas públicas.

Para Várzea Grande, são ofertadas 79 vagas, sendo 76 para ampla concorrência e três para escolas públicas.

Já no campus de Sinop estão disponíveis 245 vagas, sendo 213 para ampla concorrência e 32 para estudantes de escolas públicas

No Araguaia, são 323 vagas, sendo 286 para ampla concorrência e 37 para estudantes de escolas públicas.

Quem pode participar e como se inscrever

Podem participar candidatos que tenham feito, com aproveitamento e nota superior a zero em todas as áreas de conhecimento e na redação, pelo menos uma das dez últimas edições do Enem, entre 2016 e 2025.

A UFMT vai importar automaticamente os resultados do candidato disponibilizados pelo Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep). Para a classificação, será considerada a edição do Enem em que o estudante obteve a maior pontuação global.

As inscrições são gratuitas e devem ser feitas exclusivamente pela internet , na página oficial de ingresso da UFMT. Para participar, é necessário ter uma conta ativa no sistema GOV.BR.

A divulgação das inscrições deferidas e indeferidas está prevista para 5 de outubro. O prazo para apresentação de recursos será nos dias 6 e 7.

Os candidatos selecionados e com matrícula deferida terão o vínculo trancado em caráter especial no período letivo de 2026/2. O ingresso efetivo nas atividades acadêmicas ocorrerá no semestre letivo de 2027/1, devido ao calendário acadêmico atual da universidade.

articles.title: Penn Badgley's Wife Defends His Decision to Stop Filming Sex Scenes
articles.summary: Penn Badgley's wife Domino Kirke said it was the You actor's choice to stop performing sex scenes in his work, explaining, "It's just relational hygiene."
articles.body:
Penn Badgley 's wife Domino Kirke is shutting down gossip.

Three years after the Gossip Girl alum vowed to stop filming sex scenes , Kirke—who works as a doula—refuted rumors that she influenced his decision.

"I continue to get DMs about this thing that happened about three years ago, when my husband decided that he didn't want to do intimacy scenes anymore." she began in a Sept. 28 Instagram video . "Meaning: He didn't want to have sex. He didn't want to kiss. He didn't want to do any of that, which was really major in his industry."

"So, when he decided he didn't want to do this anymore, I was super happy for him, very proud of him because I understood how major it was," continued Kirke, who shares a 6-year-old son and 12-month-old twins with Badgley, as well as a teenage son Cassius with ex Morgan O'Kane . "It's just relational hygiene, and I strive to practice this in my career as a doula."

The 42-year-old went on to note that she's "not just Penn Badgley's wife."

"I also do things like support people in making these kinds of decisions for themselves and their careers," Kirke added. "I want to say, to those of you who still DM me about my husband deciding to do this for himself and his mental health, get over it."

Badgley first raise eyebrows when he cited his relationship with Kirke as one of the reason why he wasn't interested in performing sex scenes anymore, sharing that "fidelity in every relationship, especially in a marriage, is important to me."

"If you have a partner," he said during a 2023 appearance on Andy Cohen Live , "and you wanna be with your partner and you have to do this with another person, frankly, for me, it's just not my desire."

However, the 39-year-old later added that he was "not interested" because choreographing certain details in sex scenes made for unrealistic chemistry between the actors.

"It's just not the way sex happens, the falling against the wall and grasping at each other's clothes, all this stuff," he told The Guardian in 2025. "There's no time for condoms, there's no time for conversation. There's no time for awkwardness, for real connection."

But that's not to say Badgley's rule is set in stone. After all, the You star did engage in some hot and heavy behavior onscreen during the fifth and final season of his Netflix series.

"I had to throw that out the window," Badgley admitted in an interview with People last year. "And as I always said, I said, my desire is that least as possible, but if it's necessary, that's the show we all sign up to make. So, let's make sure it's vital, let's make sure it's important, it's deliberate. And we did."

So, what is it actually like to film a sex scene? Keep reading to see what other celebs have to say.

When it comes to onscreen nudity, the Silver Linings Playbook actress has found that her mindset has shifted over the years. Indeed, when she filmed her first nude scene in 2018's Red Sparrow , Lawrence was initially very uncomfortable with the experience. " Red Sparrow really scared the hell out of me because I get nude," she told Vanity Fair at the time. "I tried to do the movie without nudity but realized it just wouldn't be right to put the character through something that I, myself, am not willing to go through." But when it came time to film sex scenes opposite Robert Pattinson in 2025's Die My Love , she was "not sensitive" about baring it all. "I don't care about nudity," she shared during a screening of the film. "I wanted [director] Lynne [ Ramsay ] to have total freedom artistically."

The wrestler-turned-actor shared a behind-the-scenes look into his sex scene with Amy Schumer in 2015's Trainwreck . "There is nothing intimate about it," he said on an episode of Club Shay Shay in August 2024. "Nothing. So, like, it's really embarrassing." Luckily, Cena had a very understanding costar. "Amy is an angel," he continued. "She made the environment so comfortable, and then when I got the part, eventually they were like, 'Yeah, it's a sex scene and we want you to do elaborate and crazy stunt sex, and all those lines you had? We're probably not going to use them, we're just going to do this stunt sex scene.'"

The Fantastic Four alum recalled feeling incredibly uncomfortable when she filmed a scene in the 2005 movie in which her character Sue Storm appeared naked over a bridge. "I thought that was awful," Alba shared in 2025 . "It was very humiliating in real life." She added, "I grew up with a pretty conservative family, and I am a pretty modest person. I dreaded that scene for weeks. I have a lot of whiplash from those days."

While the Ocean's Eleven star had his fair share of movie romances, Clooney revealed that after a conversation with wife Amal Clooney he was no longer interested in kissing women on screen. "I've been trying to go the route Paul Newman did. 'OK, well, I'm not kissing a girl any more,'" he told the Daily Mail in 2025. "When I turned 60, I had a conversation with my wife. I said, 'Look, I can still play basketball with the boys. I play with 25-year-old guys.'" "'I can still hang, I'm in shape,'" he added. "'But in 25 years, I'm 85 years old. It doesn't matter how many granola bars you eat, that's a real number.'"

The Titanic actress has never shied away when it comes to sharing just how strange shooting sex scenes can be. "Those scenes are really awkward," Winslet told E! News in 2017 . "It doesn't matter which way you look at it." Still, after having filmed many of them over the years, she felt as though she's become a bit of a pro as she imitated herself on set, "'Ok, everyone, this is how it's going to be.'"

While Bridgerton is known for its steamy love scenes, according to the show's star, there's nothing truly sexy about filming the scenes, especially as they utilized an intimacy coordinator. "It really was like shooting a stunt, it looked real, but we've got padding on," Dynevor told Harper's Bazaar in 2021. "The angles are very … I mean, I've shot intimacy scenes before in the past without any of that. And I can't believe really how new this all is, because it just changed the game." The Fair Play alum added that she and costar Regé-Jean Page "felt super safe" after rehearsals, noting that once they got to set, "We already knew exactly what we're doing. We'd blocked it all so specifically. I knew exactly where his hand was going to go at what point. So it just meant that there wasn't any room for a director to go, 'Oh, I want to see this now.'"

articles.summary: 'Hanuman Ansh' posted a surprising late-stage surge as it enters Day 54 of its theatrical run with the Vishal Chaturvedi-directed spiritual drama on Neem
articles.body: 'Hanuman Ansh' posted a surprising late-stage surge as it enters Day 54 of its theatrical run with the Vishal Chaturvedi-directed spiritual drama on Neem Karoli Baba, led by Shobhinaw Satyaa, continuing to attract audiences well into its eighth week. After a modest opening, the film has now crossed the Rs. 400 crore mark worldwide, extending a box office run that continues to defy the usual life cycle of a theatrical release, marking a sharp turnaround from its third week onwards and has maintained an unusually long run at the box office.With its India net collection already past Rs. 309 crore, 'Hanuman Ansh' now has the Rs. 315 crore domestic mark within reach in the coming days, especially if the recent burst of momentum carries forward. On the worldwide front, with the global gross already at Rs. 404.25 crore, the film looks well placed to push towards the Rs. 410-420 crore range, further reinforcing its status as one of the most remarkable long-run success stories at the Indian box office this year.'Hanuman Ansh's domestic box office run'Hanuman Ansh' had already built a strong base of Rs. 291.53 crore in India net by the end of Day 50, having grown steadily from a slow Rs. 1.08 crore opening week through a series of extraordinary weeks that peaked with Rs. 90.25 crore in Week 5. The film then delivered a fresh jolt of momentum, adding Rs. 6.50 crore on Day 51 and a stronger Rs. 9 crore on Day 52, pushing it past the Rs. 300 crore mark to Rs. 307.03 crore. Day 53 saw a natural cooling off with Rs. 2.35 crore, taking the cumulative India net to Rs. 309.38 crore and gross collection to Rs. 365.50 crore.‘Hanuman Ansh’ overseas collection and worldwide totalInternational markets have continued to contribute small but consistent sums through this stretch of the film's run. The overseas gross moved from Rs. 37 crore after Day 50 to Rs. 37.75 crore after Day 51, then to Rs. 38.50 crore after Day 52, before adding a further Rs. 0.25 crore on Day 53 to reach Rs. 38.75 crore. Combined with its domestic numbers, this pushed the worldwide gross to Rs. 404.25 crore by the close of Day 53.'Hanuman Ansh' Day 54 collection live trackingAs per the trade tracking portal Sacnilk, 'Hanuman Ansh' is currently running across 2,606 shows on Day 54, having added Rs. 1.39 crore to its tally so far in the day.This takes the film's overall India gross to Rs. 367.04 crore and its India net to Rs. 310.67 crore, with the final Day 54 figure expected once all shows for the day have concluded.Day wise collections for 'Hanuman Ansh'Week 1: Rs. 1.08 croreWeek 2: Rs. 0.40 croreWeek 3: Rs. 10.40 croreWeek 4: Rs. 61.00 croreWeek 5: Rs. 90.25 croreWeek 6: Rs. 80.25 croreWeek 7: Rs. 44.80 croreDay 50: Rs. 3.35 croreDay 51: Rs. 6.50 croreDay 52: Rs. 9.00 croreDay 53: Rs. 2.35 croreDay 54 [LIVE]: Rs. 1.39 croreTOTAL: Rs. 310.67 croreMore about 'Hanuman Ansh'Written and directed by Vishal Chaturvedi, 'Hanuman Ansh' is a biographical spiritual drama inspired by the life of Neem Karoli Baba, also known as Maharaj Ji. The film follows his spiritual journey and explores themes of faith, devotion, compassion and selfless service.Shobhinaw Satyaa plays Neem Karoli Baba, while Purnima Tiwari portrays his wife, Rambeti Sharma. Chandan Anand, Anil Rastogi, Gulshan Pandey and Vihaan Shedge are also part of the cast.'Hanuman Ansh' was released in theatres on August 7, 2026. articles.title: Royal family unclear of Harry and Meghan’s motives as ‘frustration’ lingers: expert
articles.summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's return to the U.K. has the royal family questioning their motives as experts debate a half-in half-out role.
articles.body: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have been back in the U.K. for a month, and senior members of the royal family still don't know what their agenda is. On Sept. 16, People reported that a palace source said, "The royal family still don’t know what their motives are," just weeks after Harry and Markle officially moved overseas. Royal commentators told Fox News Digital they are divided over Harry and Meghan’s return to the U.K., with some accusing the palace of undermining the couple while others said the intervention was necessary to reaffirm that they remain private citizens and will not resume a "half-in, half-out" royal role. A little over a week after Harry and Markle made their plans to relocate back to the U.K. public, King Charles issued a letter via the Lord Chamberlain, Lord Benyon, stating that they would be classified as non-working royals. MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK RETURN POSES PALACE CONTROL ‘NIGHTMARE,’ EXPERT WARNS Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that the palace is undermining Harry and Meghan’s return while preventing them from creating royal-style events. "Harry and Meghan claim to want a private family life in Britain with access to Harry’s roots, while they repeatedly invade their own privacy." "Harry and Meghan simply want to be left in peace, allowing themselves privacy to protect their children and to cover some charity activities. The palace, I feel, are being driven by officials and maybe William to constantly undermine this return. Officially, they are making sure Harry and Meghan are not seen to be creating royal-style events," he said. According to Turner, the letter on behalf of the king was unnecessary. PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON 'PLAYING IT COOL' AS PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE RETURN TO THE UK: EXPERT "In my mind, the act of clarification was not necessary, creating humiliation for the couple and a cowardly act by those behind the letter," he began. "William may see the return as a distraction from his popularity and, as it seems already, Harry has received some favorable accolades from people he is meeting at events -- this could be an annoyance to William’s ego." Hilary Fordwich, British royal expert, told Fox News Digital that the letter on behalf of the king was just clarification on what they already agreed upon when Harry and Markle stepped away as senior royals in 2020. "Harry and Meghan claim to want a private family life in Britain with access to Harry’s roots, while they repeatedly invade their own privacy. They are retaining their independent charitable and commercial careers while also posturing themselves as working royals, which is directly thwarting the Sandringham agreement to refrain from monetizing their titles. The palace’s public intervention demonstrates the concerns surrounding their posturing with official royal type activities." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "The public clarification from King Charles III was another line in the sand, restating what was already agreed regarding the Sussexes' departure for the U.S. in 2020," Fordwich said. "The Lord Chamberlain’s letter not only stated that the Sussexes were actually not undertaking royal engagements, it reiterated no change in their status, clarified that they are no longer working royals and that their HRH styles remain in abeyance,' Fordwich noted. articles.title: “Good Morning America’”s Will Reeve Reveals Testicular Cancer Diagnosis: ‘I’ve Been Reminded What Means The Most To Me’
articles.summary: The ABC News correspondent, 34, says he was inspired by his parents’ example to share his story in hopes of helping others
articles.body:
Will Reeve opens up about his testicular cancer diagnosis and treatment, sharing his story for the first time

He credits his wife Amanda, whom he married in January, for encouraging him to seek medical attention early, which led to successful treatment

Following the example of his parents, Christopher and Dana Reeve, he says, "I was raised to share one's struggles if, in doing so, that might help others."

"I was raised to share one's struggles if, in doing so, that might help others," says ABC News national correspondent Will Reeve .

Just two years old when his father, Superman actor Christopher Reeve , was thrown from a horse and became paralyzed from the neck down, Reeve grew up watching his dad and mom, Dana Reeve , fight for spinal-cord-injury awareness and research and launch The Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation . Two years after his father died in 2004 at age 52, his mom died from lung cancer at 44.

"Watching my parents up close take the adversity they faced in their lives and repurpose it into something hopeful left a major impact on my life and how I try to live it," Reeve says.

That lesson took on new meaning this past spring after Reeve, 34, was diagnosed with testicular cancer, which then spread to the lymph nodes in his abdomen.

Currently cancer-free (as of a checkup on Sept. 8) and inspired by his parents' example, he's sharing his own cancer story now, for the first time. "I have felt so loved and supported and rooted for by family, friends and strangers alike for my entire life," says Reeve, who was 13 when his mom died and was then raised by the parents of his best friend, who lived across the street. "And that's a big part of why I wanted to speak about this. I'm going to be fine. But this was a heck of a chapter."

Reeve first noticed a tender lump on one of his testicles in the shower this past April. "I assumed it was nothing or would go away," he says. But his wife of three months, wedding and event planner, Amanda Dubin Reeve, 30, urged him to get an ultrasound ("It's probably nothing," she told him, "but what if it's something?") "I was stunned," says Reeve. In early May, he underwent an orchiectomy to remove the cancerous testicle, the standard surgical procedure for testicular cancer.

"I hadn't had surgery since I got my tonsils out at 5," says Reeve, who took a few days off work to recover. "So I was more nervous about the unknown of the surgery rather than the overwhelming realization that I would be losing an essential part of my body forever."

He credits Amanda with encouraging — and persuading — him to get checked. "We talk about 'in sickness and in health," he says. "We got an early test of our vows, just a few months in."

Adds Amanda: "The silver lining was that we had validation early in the marriage that we are well-equipped to tackle anything." He also did sperm banking, "because we do want to start a family," he notes. "And while an orchiectomy doesn't prevent natural conception, you never know, so you want to be safe."

They'd hoped it would all be just "a momentary blip in an otherwise great time in my life," recalls Reeve. But further test results revealed that 95 percent of the testicular cancer found was embryonal carcinoma, an aggressive form of the disease, leading to a six-hour surgery on June 10 to remove some dozens of lymph nodes in his abdomen.

Three of those tested positive for testicular cancer, dictating two rounds of chemotherapy. "Every doctor I saw along the way was using what I call the good C-word—'cure,'" says Reeve, who took two and a half weeks off from GMA to recover.

Still, the symmetry with his own family's history was striking.

"The irony is not lost on me that 20 years after my mom died of lung cancer at Memorial Sloan Kettering, there I was in the same building getting treated for cancer," he says. "I was experiencing life as each of my parents at the same time. Because I was a cancer patient at Memorial Sloan Kettering, I was getting a firsthand experience at what my mother went through. Simultaneously, I was learning more about what it was like to be my dad in the final nine years of his life, where he had my mom and our family taking care of him. And there I was with my wife, who, since the day I met her, has reminded me in so many ways of my mom, now playing the role of wife and caregiver."

During chemo sessions he'd head from the studios at GMA , where he's a frequent contributor, to the hospital, where he also did cold-capping to keep his hair. The helmet "looked like the under side of a manta ray," he says with a laugh. With the help of anti-nausea drugs, "I never really felt sick at all," he says, even though "some of the after effects [24-hour headaches, bone pain] felt like a bit of ailment whack-a-mole."

He finished his second round on July 31, taking a few days off after each to recover. "My colleagues at ABC are like family to me and have been with me every step of the way," he says. "I'm fortunate that I caught this early. Yes, I had to jump through some flaming hoops to get to the other side, but it could have been much worse had I ignored it or delayed going to the doctor."

Take PEOPLE with you! Subscribe to PEOPLE magazine to get the latest details on celebrity news, exclusive royal updates, how-it-happened true crime stories and more — right to your mailbox.

"The experience has taught me to pay attention to my body," says Reeve, who will initially have scans and bloodwork three to four times a year to monitor for any chance of recurrence and decrease from there. "And lean on your people," he adds. "That started for me with Amanda, but it extends to my siblings [Alexandra, 42, and Matthew Reeve, 46, from his dad's earlier relationship with Gae Exton], family, close friends and colleagues who helped carry me through."

He's also learned to "live even more intentionally and simply," as he puts it. "It's easy to get caught up in the madness of modern life and forget what's most important."

Looking back, he says, "I've had a lot happen in my life. But none of it until now had happened to me in a way. My dad got injured and then the next nine years a lot of our focus was taking care of him and making sure that we had as full and happy a life as possible, while also facing the realities of my dad being paralyzed and in a wheelchair, unable to move or breathe on his own. And then he died, and I had to learn what grief was. And shortly after that, my mom, who had never smoked, gets sick with lung cancer and then dies, and I learned grief all over again at a different level."

The loss forged an emotional connection between Reeve and the public that moves him to this day. "For all the people who care about me, I'm so grateful and also ask that any sympathy one might have be channeled into love and care for those closest to them, because we all need to love and care for the people in our lives." •

articles.summary: Fatima Sana Shaikh has spoken out against the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation’s (BMC) proposal to increase the local entertainment tax on
articles.body: Fatima Sana Shaikh has spoken out against the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation’s (BMC) proposal to increase the local entertainment tax on air-conditioned cinema halls and multiplexes in Mumbai by 570 per cent. The actress questioned whether audiences would continue visiting theatres if the proposed hike pushes up the overall cost of a movie outing.What did Fatima Sana Shaikh say about the proposed entertainment tax hike?Speaking about the proposal at NDTV Yuva 2026, Fatima pointed to the already high cost of watching a film in theatres.“Kaun dekhega fir filmein? Waise hi koi nahi dekh raha. Film dekhne jaana ho, toh 2000-3000 toh easily… 1000 ke toh popcorn hai. Kaun khayega? Matlab 10 baar sochna padega," the actress said. (Who will watch movies then? No one is watching anyway. If you want to go see a movie, it's easily Rs. 2000-3000... popcorn costs Rs. 1000. Who will eat it? You'll have to think 10 times)She further noted that movie tickets can already cost around Rs 700-800, making a family outing to the cinema an expensive proposition once food and other expenses are added.Fatima Sana Shaikh calls proposed tax hike ‘very classist’Fatima also described the proposed increase as “very classist”, arguing that the rising cost of theatrical entertainment could make cinemas less accessible to sections of the audience.“It is also very classist, I must say, because single screens are over, so you have already alienated your audience.”The actress said that many people already feel intimidated by the environment at multiplexes because they believe they do not fit in. She argued that making theatrical viewing more expensive could further widen that gap.“There are a lot of people who find going to a theatre very intimidating because they feel they don’t fit there,” she said, adding that the proposed hike was “very sad”.Fatima also emphasised the wider cultural role of cinema, saying films can be an accessible way of reaching audiences and raising questions about morality and society.“The moment you make it expensive, you are taking it away from a lot of people,” she said.Social media users back Fatima Sana ShaikhFatima’s comments also drew support from several social media users. One user wrote that her response was “very natural and accurate” and agreed with her concerns about the impact of the proposed tax hike on cinema halls in Maharashtra.Another user commented, “Finally someone who knows the reality.”Fatima Sana Shaikh’s upcoming projectsFatima was last seen in the OTT series 'Hunkaar: The Roar' in which she played a cop. articles.title: Judge Judy passed the torch to son Adam Levy with one blunt piece of advice
articles.summary: Adam Levy reveals the blunt advice his mother Judge Judy Sheindlin gave him before he took the bench on "Adam's Law" and how he confronts nepo-baby pressure.
articles.body: Judge Judy Sheindlin's son Adam Levy recalled how his famous mother displayed her trademark bluntness while encouraging him before he took the bench for his new syndicated reality court series "Adam's Law." Levy, 58, is the presiding judge on the show, which was created by Sheindlin, 83, who also serves as an executive producer through her company Queen Bee Productions. "Adam's Law" is also produced and distributed in national syndication by CBS Media Ventures. During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, Levy shared the advice that Sheindlin gave him before the television icon handed off the gavel to her son. JUDGE JUDY'S SON ADAM LEVY SAYS HE COULD FIX LOS ANGELES ‘IN A MONTH’ "She said, 'You've got this. I know you've got this. Have fun, do what you do, don't let people lead you to places where you don't feel comfortable, be true to yourself, and don't screw this up,'" Levy said with a laugh. "That's what she said." Prior to her TV fame, Sheindlin was a New York Family Court judge known for her no-nonsense courtroom style. She was appointed to The Family Court in 1982 by then Mayor Ed Koch. Sheindlin skyrocketed to fame after she was featured in a 1993 "60 Minutes" segment that introduced viewers to her tough, outspoken courtroom demeanor. She went on to star in the syndicated courtroom hit "Judge Judy" for 25 seasons from 1996 to 2021. During its run, "Judge Judy" was the highest-rated courtroom show on television, regularly drawing millions of viewers and at one point attracting an audience of 10 million. It became one of the most successful syndicated programs in TV history. After wrapping "Judge Judy" in July 2021, Sheindlin returned to the courtroom that November with the Amazon streaming series "Judy Justice." HAYDEN PANETTIERE AND THE CHILD STARS WHOSE RELATIONSHIPS WITH THEIR MOMAGERS TURNED COMPLICATED Earlier this month, Sheindlin announced that the October finale of "Judy Justice" would mark her retirement from appearing on TV, and she was passing the torch to Levy. Levy is the son of Sheindlin and her ex-husband Ronald Levy, who also share daughter Jamie. He has practiced law for 25 years and previously served two terms as the Putnam County District Attorney in New York. JUDGE ADAM LEVY PREVIEWS HIS ‘NITTY-GRITTY’ NEW SHOW – AND HOW HIS STYLE COMPARES TO HIS MOM JUDGE JUDY Before launching "Adam's Law" on Sept. 14, Levy appeared as a presiding judge on Prime Video's "Tribunal Justice" and "Justice on Trial," two courtroom series created by Sheindlin. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Levy confessed that he was worried about how his mother would judge his performance when he made his TV debut on "Tribunal Justice." He admitted to feeling pressure to live up to her legacy, and he was anxious over being labeled a "nepo baby." KAIA GERBER OWNS 'NEPO BABY' STATUS WHILE QUESTIONING OTHER CELEBRITY KIDS: 'SHOW ME WHY YOU DESERVE THIS JOB' "I was nervous," he recalled. "Not doing what I was doing, that was in my wheelhouse. I didn't want to disappoint her. And I knew that there were a lot of other people, a lot of other lawyers and judges that were just as qualified, if not more so, to be in the seat I was in." "And, but for my DNA, I would still be trying cases someplace else," he continued. "So there was a lot of pressure to prove that, and it wasn't even to myself — because I knew that, again, it was in my wheelhouse — but to show everyone, ‘Listen, I get it. I get this whole nepo baby stuff. I do.’ And I can understand why people sometimes are disappointed and angry and upset and at the offspring of famous people." "But at the same time, I just wanted people to give me a fair shot, a chance," Levy added. Levy recalled feeling relieved when Sheindlin told him that he was "a natural" after watching him on "Tribunal Justice." "When she saw me for the first time, she said, 'There, now you know. Now you've got nothing to worry about.' And that was nice to hear," he said. Levy told Fox News Digital that while Sheindlin has never criticized the rulings that he makes on his shows, she has sometimes shared how she would have handled the cases differently. He explained that the two regularly discuss his cases and Sheindlin is continuing to actively mentor him. JUDGE JUDY PREPARING TO END DECADES-LONG RUN AS TV'S TOUGHEST JUDGE "She's hands-on," he said. "She's not retired. She is rewired. So, while she may not be in front of the camera anymore, that does not mean that she has removed herself from the courtroom genre." "She and I discussed many of the cases before they are tried and when they are taped," Levy continued. "We will go over the facts of the case. We will go all over the legal issues, the moral issues, we will go over the background information that I have uncovered and how, if at all, to use it during the trial." Levy said that his discussions with Sheindlin were in keeping with a tradition that his family members, many of whom include prosecutors and defense attorneys, carried on for 30 years. "Whenever we had cases, we would go out to dinner as a family," he recalled. "And we would — whoever was on trial, we would bring our case file, and we would throw it in the middle of the table." "Everyone would take a piece, and we'd review it," Levy continued. "We would find the strengths and the weaknesses and how to go about arguing the issues before — whether it was a bench trial with a judge or a jury. I mean, that's what we did." JUDGE JUDY WARNS OF 'DANGER' IF PROSECUTORS DON'T RETRY LINDSAY CLANCY AFTER MURDER TRIAL ENDS IN MISTRIAL "And that's what I do now with Judy," he added. "So I think it's seamless. The process is seamless. That's what we do." Levy explained that his judicial style is "a bit different" than that of his mother, though viewers will also recognize certain similarities. "It is still about taking personal responsibility for yourself, doing the right thing, telling the truth when you're in court — all of those things are the same," he said. "The way that I go about it though is my own style. It's a little more understanding at times, I think, but when someone comes in to court and misrepresents their case or lies, that's when you'll see the DNA come out." Levy also shared that his approach to the litigants who appear before him in court was influenced by his upbringing under Sheindlin's watchful eye. He told Fox News Digital that he and his sister Jamie could "never" get away with anything while they were growing up. JUDGE JUDY SAYS THOSE WHO DON'T LIKE AMERICA SHOULD 'GO SOMEWHERE ELSE' "I kid around, and I say, hundreds of millions of people have watched her over the last 30 years. And they see a tough lady, a tough judge, cutting through the nonsense, and they see it every day," he said. "I, when I saw her on TV, would say, 'Yeah, that's exactly who I grew up with. Exactly.'" "And when the litigants would say something that offended her sense of common sense, or said something that was demonstrably false, I could sympathize with that litigant because I, as a kid, would try to do the same thing," Levy continued. "And when they would say it, I would just close my eyes and wince because I knew what was coming. And she never disappointed me while watching her on the show." "But in all fairness, at the same time, I also remember when things would happen, and I would tell the truth as a child, as a teenager, and she did not believe something I said that was the truth," he shared. "And I remembered how that felt. And so with that in mind, as I'm doing the show now, as part of my own style, is not to so quickly reject something someone says if it sounds or if it would seem to be inconsistent with common sense." "Sometimes, things happen that are inconsistent with commonsense," Levy noted. "Everyday life, things just — you get a curveball. And just because you get a curveball, and you respond to that curveball in a certain way doesn't mean that — and you tell about it — doesn't mean that you're lying." Levy explained that his childhood experiences led him to make a major format change to "Adam's Law" that differentiated the series from his mother's courtroom shows. On "Judge Judy," Sheindlin generally questioned litigants and reviewed the case file as the proceedings unfolded on camera. She would receive the case materials at the start of each hearing, summarize the dispute, and then question the parties, with much of the evidence being introduced during the televised proceeding. However, Levy said that he built more time into his process so he could thoroughly vet each case before litigants stepped into his courtroom. "I insisted on changing the format to requiring the litigant to provide their evidence before they come to the show so that I could review it," he said. "And if something did seem off, I was able to examine it, do a background check on it." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "I was able to spend a little more time or no — I could spend a lot more time," Levy continued. "Sometimes it would take me a day, one full day, to review one case that would end up 17 minutes on TV." "It would take me 48 hours sometimes to go through it to make sure that, at least to me, I got it right. Because I didn't want to accuse someone of being a liar, where they were really telling the truth." When asked who between himself and his mother would be more likely to show mercy if they heard the exact same case separately, Levy had a definitive answer. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? articles.title: New York Magazine's first 'Men's Style' issue features shirtless trans actor Elliot Page
articles.summary: Elliot Page appears shirtless in New York Magazine's first-ever men's style issue, sparking fierce debate over masculinity and fashion coverage.
articles.body: New York Magazine has released a new men’s style issue, a first for the company, and decided to feature the transgender actor and biological female Elliot Page. In an article headlined "The Men’s Style Issue," the magazine recalled its history covering men's fashion. "Over the years, we have often returned to the subject of men’s style. There was the 1971 cover story wondering if men would get into high heels for fall and the 1996 profile of male supermodels (‘They’re hot, they’re rich, they’re openly straight,’ read the cover line)," the magazine wrote. "For several seasons starting in 2006, the back half of the women’s fashion issue was a mini men’s magazine and featured a baby Thom Browne fresh off his first CFDA Award win and metrosexuals done up in their aughts finery sipping Peronis at Bungalow 8." "Now, 20 years later — when even 15-year-olds are ‘hype’ about Ralph, Armani’s got a brand-new designer, and a pair of worn Chrome Hearts jeans can go for $100,000 — feels like the right moment to devote a special issue to men’s style: the power players shaping the business, the new characters shaking up the scene, the old ‘semi-supermodels’ who are still around," the magazine continued. "We stopped short of announcing another revolution in men’s clothes, though you may soon find guys sauntering through the city in sarongs." ELLIOT PAGE CLAIMS NO ACTING OFFERS ARISE AFTER 'THE ODYSSEY,' HINTS TRANSITION MAY BE WHY The issue featured multiple covers, including one with Page, and linked to an article headlined "The Boys in the Baths." The magazine described the piece as "Shvitzing and kibitzing with some of New York's most stylish men at the East Village's Russian & Turkish Baths." Page was among numerous others featured largely unclothed and described the bathhouse experience. "I went to a bathhouse recently. I’ve only in the past couple of years been like, 'Yeah, that sounds nice, to like go somewhere and sit around in your body like that.' I do sing in the shower sometimes," Page said. "The same songs and lyrics will get stuck in my head, and I don’t know why. Like ‘Do you believe in life after love?’ That’s one I’ll belt out. Or ‘The Sound of Music’: I’ve never seen the movie, which seems crazy, but for some reason I find myself belting out that song in the shower. I can’t explain it." Political commentator Link Lauren criticized the magazine for promoting a biological female in a male space, arguing that displays of masculinity are already rare in the media. "There is a shortage of masculinity in mainstream media, and for years masculinity itself has been degraded and dismissed as ‘toxic.’ Now New York Magazine launches its first-ever men’s style issue with Elliot Page shirtless, wearing little more than a flimsy necklace with visible mastectomy scars. It’s supposedly about fashion, yet there are barely any clothes. They knew this cover would generate attention and controversy. I don’t think they actually care about men or style — they care about clicks. If it weren’t for 'transitioning' we wouldn’t even be talking about this actor. They hadn’t been relevant in years." DANA WHITE MOCKS CONCERNS ABOUT SO-CALLED 'TOXIC MASCULINITY,' WARNS SOCIETY HAS 'DISPLACED' YOUNG MEN Tim Graham, executive editor of media watchdog NewsBusters, blasted the magazine for its choice. "My first reaction is this: I thought these New York Magazine people are the smartest graduates from the best journalism schools, and they can't figure out who is a man and who is a woman for a ‘Men's Style’ feature. They want to pretend that this guy is a slightly thinner Channing Tatum who could dance in a Magic Mike sequel. They want to pretend none of [us] remember Ellen Page playing pregnant in ‘Juno.’" He concluded by saying that this is part of a larger phenomenon: "Obviously, they seem like they're borrowing from Glamour magazine making a ‘trans woman’ model one of their ‘Women of the Year’ a while back. They're striking a woke pose and they expect a round of progressive applause." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: ‘Saved by the Bell’ star Dennis Haskins dead at 75
articles.summary: Dennis Haskins first portrayed Mr. Belding on "Good Morning, Miss Bliss" before the role became iconic across the "Saved by the Bell" franchise.
articles.body: Dennis Haskins, the actor best known for playing Bayside High School Principal Richard Belding on the hit sitcom "Saved by the Bell," has died. He was 75. Haskins' representative confirmed his death to Fox News Digital, saying, "It’s a tragic loss. Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis loved him even more. He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans. He always had time for them, no matter what. He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly. I’m heartbroken." His cause of death is currently unknown. HOLLYWOOD STARS WHO DIED IN 2026: PHOTOS Haskins' former "Saved by the Bell" co-stars are remembering the actor following his death. Mario Lopez, who played A.C. Slater, was among those to pay tribute to Haskins, remembering his former co-star as someone who brought a playful energy to the set despite portraying Bayside High's principal. "Heartbroken to hear about my old friend Dennis Haskins. He played the principal, but Dennis was the biggest kid on the SBTB set. If you knew him, you loved him—and if there was karaoke, you knew Dennis was getting on that mic! I’m grateful for the laughs, the memories, and the friendship we shared all these years. Rest easy, my friend. You’ll always be part of our Bayside family," he wrote in a heartfelt social media post. Lark Voorhies, who played Lisa Turtle on the hit sitcom, shared an emotional tribute on Instagram, reflecting on her nearly 40-year friendship with Haskins. Voorhies called him a "fabulous person, a loyal friend, and someone with such a kind, gentle heart," and said she would miss his warmth and laughter. Her tribute highlighted the longtime bond between the cast members, who remained connected decades after the original series ended. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Haskins was born Nov. 18, 1950, in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He became one of the most recognizable faces of the "Saved by the Bell" franchise, portraying the often-exasperated Principal Belding as he tried to keep Zack Morris, portrayed by Mark-Paul Gosselaar, and his fellow Bayside students in line. His journey as Mr. Belding began before "Saved by the Bell" officially hit NBC. articles.title: Sylvester Stallone Says Henry Winkler Showed Up ‘Like a Godsend’ When He Arrived in Hollywood with ‘Barely $500’
articles.summary: The actor recalls the ‘Happy Days’ star helping him and his first wife find an affordable motel after they first came to Los Angeles
articles.body:
Sylvester Stallone and Henry Winkler became friends while filming The Lords of Flatbush with Perry King

Winkler helped Stallone and Sasha Czack find an affordable motel after their cross-country move

Stallone recounts his early Hollywood struggles in The Steps: A Memoir , out now

Sylvester Stallone may have had a rough start in Hollywood, but he had a friend waiting in the wings.

Long before he became one of the biggest action stars in the world, Stallone, 80, was a struggling actor trying to make it in Los Angeles. Along the way, he found an unlikely friend in Henry Winkler , who would ultimately offer a helping hand when Stallone needed it most.

In his new book, The Steps: A Memoir , Stallone recalls the two first crossing paths while working on The Lords of Flatbush , after Winkler, 80, joined the cast alongside the Rocky actor and Perry King. Stallone says he and Winkler hit it off right away, despite their very different backgrounds.

"We were an odd couple. He was an intellectual Jewish kid from the Upper West Side who graduated from the Yale School of Drama-the real deal. I had to learn everything the hard way," Stallone writes. "We were anomalies in each other's lives. To see us together was like watching a zebra hang out with a buffalo. Still, we clicked, because Henry is a genuinely wonderful human being."

Winkler soon got a glimpse of just how difficult Stallone's circumstances were. When he visited Stallone's shabby apartment, he saw the struggling actor's modest surroundings — and the stack of screenplays Stallone hoped would eventually change his life.

Years later, Stallone would find himself in an even more precarious position when he and his wife, Sasha Czack , made the cross-country trip to California. They didn't have a place to live, Stallone barely knew the city, and after arriving in Los Angeles, they had just one person to call: The Fonz .

By then, Winkler had moved to California and become a star thanks to Happy Days . Stallone pulled up near Hollywood and Vine, taking in the famous sights before realizing he had no idea where to go next.

"The only choice I had was to call my friend, Henry Winkler, who I hadn't talked to for more than a year," he writes. "Like a god-send, he showed up a little while later and was nice enough to direct us to a motel that we could afford for maybe two nights."

Stallone writes that Winkler also shared stories about his own struggles establishing himself in Hollywood, giving the actor a much-needed boost of confidence.

By the time Stallone and Sasha left the motel, they were still living on a shoestring budget.

"We had barely $500 left of the $830 we departed New York with," Stallone remembers.

Winkler pointed them toward the San Fernando Valley, where they eventually found a tiny rental in Encino for $300 a month, Stallone writes. It wasn't glamorous — the house was barely 500 square feet, with no grass and no air-conditioning — but it gave Stallone a place to begin building the career he had dreamed about.

And he didn't have to wait long for that dream to become reality.

When Stallone first arrived at Hollywood and Vine, he had no idea that the nearby Walk of Fame would one day bear his name.

"That I would have a star there less than ten years later, and only a few blocks away, still boggles my mind," he writes.

articles.title: Actor nominated for film Albert credits beautiful Guernsey
articles.summary: James Howard says Guernsey is punching above its weight in the film industry.
articles.body:
An actor nominated for his role in a short film set and shot entirely in Guernsey has credited the island as a principal "character" in the piece.

Set against the island's windswept cliffs in the 17th Century, Albert follows the tale of Sarre, a reclusive man and his forbidden book Le Petit Albert .

James Howard plays a rector in the film and has been nominated for Best Supporting Actor at the Quest film festival in Utah, United States of America - the latest in a series of industry nods for its creators.

Howard said: "It just shows the amount of talent that went into making the film on-island and goes to show how Guernsey is punching above its weight."

He said: "It's a lovely film, only about 17 minutes long, which tells a really lovely story, and it does a wonderful job of showing Guernsey at its best."

On his nomination, Howard said: "I was blown away, really surprised, it's totally unexpected.

"I'm really delighted but more than anything, I'm delighted the film is getting the recognition."

He said the film had been recognised for its cinematography, while its director G.R. Fletcher , from Guernsey, had also received a nod.

Meanwhile, the film also won Best Historical Short at the New Renaissance Film Festival in London.

"It's lovely to see the film come to life and be seen by audiences and liked by audiences as well," Howard said.

"And Guernsey comes across beautifully - it's mean, it's moody, the way it's shot - it's all done on the south coast, we had some fantastic locations," he added.

Howard, originally from Jersey, said he used his previous experience playing the "mysterious and brooding" Draco Malfoy in London's Harry Potter stage play.

In the film, Howard's character tries to help a man – played by Guernsey-born actor Cameron Ashplant – rid himself of an indestructible book.

"It's based on a real life book... a folklore tale of old," said Howard.

"I read the script, loved the script and jumped on board."

Describing Ashplant as a "fantastic local actor", he said the pair found the "right energy" to make the film work.

He said the role had been his first screen job in a decade, having devoted the intervening period to stage performances.

Describing the film as having "four characters", he said they were Ashplant, himself, Guernsey and the book on which the story was based.

articles.title: U2 rinde homenaje a Rosalía tras quedar "asombrados" por 'LUX': "Es una artista extraordinaria"
articles.standfirst: La banda irlandesa dedica a la catalana una de las canciones de su próximo álbum, 'Carnaval de Luz', y Bono reconoce que su último trabajo les ha servido de inspiración
articles.summary: La banda irlandesa dedica a la catalana una de las canciones de su próximo álbum, 'Carnaval de Luz', y Bono reconoce que su último trabajo les ha servido de inspiración
articles.body: Rosalía se ha convertido en una de las grandes fuentes de inspiración para U2. Bono, vocalista de la legendaria banda irlandesa, ha confirmado que 'The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)', una de las canciones de su próximo disco, 'Carnaval de Luz', está dedicada a Rosalía, a quien considera una "artista extraordinaria". El cantante también ha reconocido su fascinación por 'LUX', el último álbum de la artista catalana, que asegura que le ha sorprendido e inspirado profundamente. U2 publicará el próximo 13 de noviembre 'Carnaval de Luz', su decimosexto álbum de estudio y el primero que edita en nueve años. Entre las canciones que integran el disco figura 'The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)', un título que había alimentado las especulaciones sobre una posible referencia a la cantante española. Bono ha despejado finalmente cualquier duda en una entrevista con Rolling Stone: "Normalmente escribimos canciones sobre gente muerta o en prisión (...) Héroes fallecidos, o intentando sacarles de la cárcel. Esto es simplemente celebrar a alguien por ser una artista extraordinaria". El vocalista de U2 quiso contar con el visto bueno de Rosalía antes de publicar una canción que lleva su nombre. Para conseguirlo recurrió a una amiga común, la actriz española Penélope Cruz, que le animó a ponerse en contacto directamente con la cantante. Bono asegura que Rosalía le ha hecho "reír un montón" y que ambos han intercambiado mensajes y conversado sobre su admiración por Federico García Lorca. Pese a esa relación a distancia, todavía no han tenido ocasión de conocerse personalmente. "Ahora mismo no podría conocerla. Estoy reuniendo valor para enviarle la mezcla final", bromeó el cantante. Bono reconoce haberse quedado especialmente sorprendido por 'LUX', el último trabajo de Rosalía, hasta el punto de sentir que la catalana se había adelantado a U2 en algunas de las cuestiones que la banda quería explorar musicalmente. "Ha llegado al mismo punto justo antes que nosotros, lo cual es molesto, y a la vez muy inspirador", explicó. Para Bono, Rosalía comparte con U2 una misma aspiración: "utilizar el arte para contribuir al reencantamiento del mundo". 'The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)' nació originalmente en 2017 y necesitó hasta 196 versiones antes de encontrar el significado que finalmente ha llegado al disco. El productor del álbum, Garrett 'Jacknife' Lee, recuerda que en un momento del proceso se preguntó por qué estaban escribiendo una canción sobre Rosalía y qué relevancia tenía la referencia. La respuesta de Bono está relacionada con el concepto del espejo y con la manera en que la sociedad contemporánea se enfrenta al narcisismo. La canción habla, según el músico, de la facilidad con la que las personas pueden "perderse en el espejo", pero también de aquellos artistas capaces de atravesarlo para descubrir qué hay al otro lado. "Rosalía es una de ellas", afirma Bono, que relaciona esa actitud con una concepción del ser humano como cuerpo, alma y espíritu. El cantante destaca, además, la manera en que la artista catalana aborda estas cuestiones con "valentía y sentido del humor". Musicalmente, según la descripción de Rolling Stone, 'The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)' comienza con un riff acústico de guitarra y Bono imitando la voz de soprano de Rosalía. La idea inicial llegó incluso a contemplar que fuera la propia catalana quien participara en la canción. Sin embargo, el grupo acabó descartándolo con humor. "¿Por qué alguien cantaría una canción sobre sí misma? ¡Escúchame cantar sobre lo genial que soy!", ironizó el productor. Así, U2 ha terminado convirtiendo a Rosalía en protagonista de una canción que funciona a la vez como homenaje y reconocimiento artístico hacia una de las creadoras que más ha impresionado a Bono en los últimos años.

articles.title: National museums to stay free to all visitors, government says
articles.summary: It follows discussions about whether charging tourists could boost museums' finances.
articles.body:
Overseas visitors will not be charged to enter England's national museums after ministers decided against changing the universal free admission policy.

It comes after months of discussions between the government, museums, the tourism sector and local leaders to examine whether making tourists from abroad pay could boost the institutions' finances.

In March, the government said it would explore charging international visitors to enter national museums as it looks for ways to tackle funding pressures.

But the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has now said this could deter domestic visitors and that any benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector.

The UK's 15 national museums, including 12 in London, have been free for all to enter since 2001.

But a review published last year by former Labour minister Baroness Margaret Hodge suggested that a charging model for international tourists "would align the UK with other countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore".

On Tuesday, DCMS confirmed free admission to these museums would remain in place for everyone.

"The government believes that charging overseas visitors could deter domestic visitors and that the impacts and benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector and therefore will not introduce charges for overseas visitors," a spokesperson said.

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Our museums are the places that light up the world.

"That's why they must be free, forever, for everyone to access."

The DCMS said national museums contribute more than £1bn a year to the economy and attract visitors from around the world, with the Natural History Museum and the British Museum drawing 7.1 million and 6.4 million visitors respectively in 2025.

The Natural History Museum's director Dr Doug Gurr said although his museum would have benefitted from charging, the sector would have lost out overall.

"Free museums aren't a cost to the economy - they're a key reason the economy benefits from tourism in the first place," he said.

"So, we're delighted to remain free but given the visitors we bring there's a strong case for reinvesting a share of any tourism revenues in the institutions that help attract them."

Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, said: "When the British Museum was founded as the world's first public national museum in 1753 it was to be free for 'all persons'.

"So, we are delighted by the government's announcement that free entry for all will be maintained.

"This will allow everyone to enjoy and have access to our great museums across the nation as one of the things this country does so brilliantly."

The government also pointed to £760m in funding for museums through its £1.5bn Arts Everywhere Fund, as well as £600m in infrastructure funding for national museums.

It said the £13.6m museum transformation programme would help organisations move towards more sustainable business models, while ministers would work with the Arts Council and the sector on a long-term strategic plan for museums, with further details to be announced.

articles.title: In 1989, Basinger bought a town in Georgia for $20 million before selling it five years later
articles.summary: Hollywood star Kim Basinger once made an extraordinary real-estate investment in her home state of Georgia.
articles.body: Hollywood star Kim Basinger once made an extraordinary real-estate investment in her home state of Georgia. In 1989, the actress led an investment group that paid a reported $20 million for roughly 1,800 acres in and around the small town of Braselton, northeast of Atlanta. Her ambitious plan was to transform the historic community into a tourist and entertainment destination featuring movie and recording studios, boutiques and a film festival. The project, however, never came to fruition, and Basinger eventually sold the investment for a reported $1 million in 1993.Basinger had a personal connection to the Georgia townBraselton was not a random choice for Basinger. The actress was a Georgia native who grew up in nearby Athens, making the community a familiar part of the area where she was raised.At the time of the purchase, Braselton was a small community with around 500 residents. The town had been established in the 19th century by the Braselton family, and members of the family had retained extensive ownership and involvement in the community for generations.The Braselton family had reportedly been trying to sell its holdings since the early 1980s. According to a 1989 UPI report, the family ultimately agreed to Basinger’s proposal after 18 months of negotiations.Although the story is often simplified to say that Basinger “bought a town,” the transaction was actually a purchase of a substantial portion of Braselton’s real estate and commercial holdings.Contemporary reports gave slightly different acreage figures. A study reported that the deal included the town’s supermarket, bank, stores, a 600-acre industrial park and another 1,200 acres of real estate. The Los Angeles Times described the acquisition as approximately 1,800 acres and said it included the water and sewer system, an industrial park, several businesses and about 50 homes and other buildings.The deal therefore did not mean Basinger literally owned every property in the municipality or controlled its local government. Instead, she and her investment partners acquired a large portion of the town’s property and commercial assets.The idea attracted significant attention because it combined Basinger’s Hollywood career with a very unusual hometown investment.The $20 million deal involved an investment groupAnother detail that is frequently lost in retellings is that Basinger did not act entirely alone.By February 1990, the Los Angeles Times reported that American Information Technologies, or Ameritech, had joined Basinger in the investment and helped pay the $20 million price tag. The precise terms of their partnership were not publicly disclosed.The same report said the investment covered approximately 1,700 acres and included a bank, an industrial park, around 50 other buildings and frontage along Interstate 85. A movie studio was among the tentative development ideas.That distinction matters because the popular version of the story that Basinger simply spent $20 million of her own money to purchase an entire town doesn’t fully reflect the documented structure of the transaction.The ambitious development never materializedThe proposed transformation of Braselton did not happen as Basinger had imagined.Her financial difficulties were unfolding alongside a major legal battle over the film Boxing Helena. Basinger had withdrawn from the project, leading to a lawsuit by Main Line Pictures. A jury initially awarded the company more than $8 million in damages, a judgment that contributed to Basinger’s bankruptcy proceedings before an appellate court later overturned the award because of problems with the jury instructions.The financial pressure surrounding Basinger’s bankruptcy also affected assets connected to the Braselton investment. A report described the partnership as having taken on significant debt for the 1989 acquisition and said Basinger had planned to develop the property with film and recording facilities.From a Hollywood project to a piece of Georgia historyBasinger’s Braselton venture ultimately became a short-lived chapter in the community’s much longer history.The town itself continued developing after her departure. Braselton eventually expanded beyond its earlier boundaries and attracted major businesses and residential development. Today, the community is substantially larger than the small Georgia town Basinger encountered in 1989.The entertainment destination Basinger envisioned never came to life, but her unusual investment remains one of the most memorable episodes in Braselton’s modern history.What began in 1989 as a $20 million attempt to turn roughly 1,800 acres of a small Georgia community into a tourism and entertainment destination ended just four years later with the investment being sold for a reported $1 million. The episode remains a striking example of how dramatically a celebrity-backed real-estate venture can change course.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: In 2011, Taylor Swift purchased her former Beverly Hills estate where she wrote ‘1989’; the 1.5-acre property is now on the market for $7.995 million after renovations, featuring four bedrooms and five bathrooms
articles.summary: Taylor Swift’s connection to Beverly Hills real estate is back in the spotlight, with the sprawling estate she once called home now on the market for
articles.body: Taylor Swift’s connection to Beverly Hills real estate is back in the spotlight, with the sprawling estate she once called home now on the market for $7,995,000.Swift purchased the historic Pillsbury Estate in 2011 and went on to write her acclaimed pop album 1989 at the property. The 1.5-acre mini-compound has now been listed by its current owners, fashion designer Nicolas Bijan and interior designer Roxy Bijan.Built for the Pillsbury family in 1941, the Beverly Hills estate features a four-bedroom, five-bathroom layout spread across a three-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom main residence and a one-bedroom, one-bathroom guest house.The property also boasts a motor court with room for eight cars, more than a dozen mature live oak trees and a pickleball court.The Bijans purchased the estate from Swift in an off-market transaction in 2018. Since then, they have undertaken significant renovations throughout the home, giving the historic property a more contemporary look while retaining elements of its original character.Their stylish transformation even caught the attention of Architectural Digest, which featured the residence in 2021.The estate was featured in Taylor Swift’s ‘73 Questions’Swifties may also recognize the property from Swift’s famous Vogue “73 Questions” video interview.For Nicolas Bijan, the home's creative history was one of its most appealing qualities. He recalled discovering a beautiful piano in the home office when he and Roxy moved in.“When we moved in, there was a beautiful piano in the home office. I couldn’t help but be inspired by what had happened in that room,” Bijan told Page Six Hollywood.He revealed that he subsequently launched his fashion brand, NB44, from the same space.“You can tell beautiful things have happened here. I hope the next person that lives there will feel creatively inspired,” he added.A home filled with Hollywood and music historyThe property has also played an important role in the Bijans’ personal lives. The couple married at the estate in 2020 after their planned Lake Como wedding was cancelled because of the COVID-19 pandemic.They have since started a family and welcomed two children.Despite the extensive renovations and the couple’s own design choices, one notable reminder of Swift’s time at the property remains in the garden.An olive tree planted by Swift’s former boyfriend, DJ Calvin Harris, is still standing on the estate. The tree now sits among Roxy Bijan’s hot-pink roses, creating one of the few visible links to the property’s past as Swift’s Beverly Hills home.With its celebrity history, expansive grounds and extensive renovations, the Pillsbury Estate is once again seeking a new owner - nearly a decade after Swift sold the property to the Bijans.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Sylvester Stallone reacts to 'I Play Rocky' biopic; says, 'I'm not dead yet, aren't we jumping the gun a little bit?'
articles.summary: Sylvester Stallone has reacted to 'I Play Rocky', the upcoming biopic on the making of the 1976 classic 'Rocky'.
articles.body: Sylvester Stallone has reacted to 'I Play Rocky', the upcoming biopic on the making of the 1976 classic 'Rocky'. He admitted he first wondered whether his life story was being told too soon. The Hollywood icon was speaking about the same while promoting his new memoir 'The Steps'.Sylvester Stallone says, 'Aren't we jumping the gun?'According to The Hollywood Reporter, Sylvester Stallone was speaking at 92NY on Monday and said he was "kind of mixed" about the project because, as he put it, "I'm not dead yet. Aren't we jumping the gun a little bit?"Directed by Peter Farrelly, the film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival earlier this month. It features Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone and shows how the actor developed 'Rocky' and pushed it through a turbulent production.Impressed by Anthony IppolitoSylvester Stallone said his feelings changed after he saw Ippolito's work. He recalled, "I actually thought it was me the first moment; there were a couple of angles. I go to my daughter and say, 'That's unbelievable.'"He stressed that he had no role in the making of the film. "I said, 'I'll just sit back and watch.' I talked to the kid. I said, 'If you want any questions, here I am,' and that was it. But they did it all on their own," Stallone said.He also joked about seeing his mannerisms on screen. He said, "I go, 'Do I talk like that?' Now I get it. Now I get it."A recut of 'Rocky V'?Sylvester Stallone spoke about his mixed feelings on watching the 'Rocky' films today. He said, "It's like you look at a photo of yourself; everyone else likes it, but you go [growl]."He revealed that he is trying to get Amazon to let him recut the 1990 film 'Rocky V', which he described as "a thorn in my side.""It bothers me to death because I know I took my foot off the gas," he said. He added that he should have directed the film himself and "I should have been more aware of not trying to be cool to the audience."If he gets the chance, Stallone joked, "It's not going to be great. It'll be acceptable."Hollywood then and nowModerator Tracy Smith of CBS Sunday Morning asked whether Stallone could reach the top of Hollywood if he were starting out today. He said the industry has changed a great deal. "It's a whole different ideology out there… I don't think so. It's a whole different mindset," he said, as cited by The Hollywood Reporter.Stallone also said the cultural context around older films makes them hard to recreate, and he gave 'The Godfather' as an example. "For example, if you were going to make The Godfather today, try casting it. Impossible," he said. He added, "The whole premise… it just came at a certain time, and that's why it makes it so unique."He said remakes can overlook the social and cultural circumstances in which the original films were made.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Héctor Bellerín confirma la historia de 'Los Javis' y cuenta por qué rechazó 'La bola negra': "Me parecía un poco intrusismo laboral"
articles.standfirst: El futbolista del Real Betis, Héctor Bellerín, podría haber actuado en el film de Javier Ambrossi y Javier Calvo en un papel que al final defendió Miguel Bernardeau
articles.summary: El futbolista del Real Betis, Héctor Bellerín, podría haber actuado en el film de Javier Ambrossi y Javier Calvo en un papel que al final defendió Miguel Bernardeau
articles.body: Javier Ambrossi y Javier Calvo redactaron el papel de Rafael Rodríguez Rapún para su película 'La bola negra' pensando en que lo interpretara Héctor Bellerín. Aunque el futbolista del Real Betis, que rechazó la propuesta, ha vuelto a dar una lección de coherencia y empatía al revelar los motivos a pesar de ser contactado directamente por el equipo de selección de la película. Durante su intervención en el programa 'Los Javis', el futbolista explicó cómo se gestó la oportunidad: "Me contactaron en su día las organizadoras del de los castings y siempre he tenido en mi entorno mucha gente que que se dedica a la industria. Tengo gente en mi entorno que son actores, actrices... y bueno, sé que es un una industria muy complicada", dijo en una entrevista en la Cadena SER en el programa 'Libre y Directo'. Consciente de las dificultades estructurales que atraviesa el sector cultural en España, Bellerín argumentó las razones éticas que sustentaron su decisión: "Son trabajos súper precarios, es una de las industrias con más tasas de paro en nuestro país y dedican muchísimas horas y siguen teniendo una vida súper precaria. Entonces me parecía un poco intrusismo laboral. El yo simplemente por por ser quien soy, tener la oportunidad de participar en una superproducción". El lateral no dudó en celebrar el resultado final del proyecto audiovisual sin su participación, valorando positivamente el trabajo del elenco elegido: "Y es algo que... claro y mira, ha salido muy bien sin mí, ¿no? Así que igual fue una muy buena decisión". Por último, el jugador verdiblanco reiteró su profunda consideración hacia el trabajo de los intérpretes: "Pero bueno, para mí fue un honor que contactaran conmigo, me hizo muchísima ilusión y es algo que claro que creo que puede atraer a cualquiera. Pero para eso creo que hay que dedicarle muchas horas, el respeto que se merece y las horas que hay que dedicarle para poder estar en en un lugar como ese y no me creía que yo era la persona indicada para hacerlo".

articles.title: Tallulah Willis kisses father Bruce Willis on the forehead in a sweet Instagram post, weeks after sharing a health update: 'So cute'
articles.summary: Tallulah Willis has shared a rare and tender moment with her father, Bruce Willis, on Instagram.
articles.body: Tallulah Willis has shared a rare and tender moment with her father, Bruce Willis, on Instagram. The youngest daughter of Bruce and Demi Moore, 32, posted the photo on Monday, September 28. It shows her kissing the 71-year-old 'Die Hard' actor on the forehead.A sweet role reversalIn the picture, Tallulah Willis stands above her father and gently holds his head as she kisses him. The star of 'The Fifth Element' has his eyes closed, as if soaking up the moment. She captioned the post, "So cute!" and it is a role reversal from other photos she has shared of her dad kissing her on the head.Update on Bruce Willis' healthThe post comes nearly a month after Tallulah gave an update on her father's health. His family announced his diagnosis of aphasia in 2022 and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) in 2023. According to Cleveland Clinic, FTD is a broad term for brain disorders that affect the frontal and temporal lobes and can cause speech problems, emotional difficulties and personality changes. Aphasia is a language disorder caused by damage to the parts of the brain that control speech and understanding.At the end of August, the Los Angeles-based entrepreneur and artist said her father is "doing the same in terms of the last we kind of updated, which I'm told is good," Tallulah shared. "But whatever kind of day it is, my family and I meet him where he's at."Tallulah Willis on visiting her fatherShe also told PEOPLE that spending "some time with him" is part of her routine. When she visits, she said it is important for her "to go into it open to what the visit is, and knowing that before I go in, I'm solid. I'm okay.""I've done what I need to do to make sure that I can just be present," she added.Bruce Willis at Tallulah Willis's weddingBruce was also present at Tallulah Willis's August 8 wedding to Justin Acee. Vogue shared several photos from the ceremony on Instagram, including one of the newlyweds with Bruce and some behind-the-scenes moments. In a black-and-white picture, Bruce smiles with one arm around Tallulah as she leans into him, while Acee holds his other hand.Bruce and Demi Moore also share daughters Rumer and Scout. He has two more daughters, Mabel and Evelyn, with his wife, Emma Heming Willis.Tallulah's earlier words on her fatherTallulah has spoken openly about her father's diagnosis over the years. In 2024, she told PEOPLE, "It's hard. There's painful days, but there's so much love. And it's really shown me to not take any moment for granted, and I really do think that we'd be best friends. I think he's very proud of me."Tallulah has not yet announced her next project.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. Download the TOI app.Give your child the gift of confidence!
